item.title: Carnegie Mellon is putting computer science courses on YouTube for free
item.description:
Source: www.cs.cmu.edu

Top Comment:

Hi! I'm Phillip Compeau, I teach in Carnegie Mellon's Griffin School of Computer Science, and I run CS Learn, which launched today.

We're releasing full semesters of lectures from current CMU computer science courses across a variety of topics, with one course premiering each day this week. More courses come in January.

Yes, MIT got here 25 years ago :). What I'm excited about is how we're doing it: a few of our students built tools that automate a lot of the production work, so a small team can get a course out quickly and still have people review every lecture.

We'll have lots more coming across a wide array of subjects. I'd love to know if there are topics you would like to see us cover!

item.title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
item.description:
Source: calif.io

Top Comment:

From the section on performing heap grooming over the network ("Remote Heap Feng Shui"):

> The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target.

And the "Limitations" section:

> There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot.

Based on the complexity and constraints, short-term mass-exploitation seems unlikely. It will take some time before there are reliable exploits, and they may require running on infra close to the target.

But a long tail of unpatched java applications/services at high-value targets getting exploited, seems plausible to me.

item.title: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down
item.description:
Source: www.cnn.com

https://www.reuters.com/technology/highly-classified-us-nati...

Top Comment:

I feel like something started after Elon purchased twitter and made all those personnel deep cuts. In the era prior, it wasn't too hard to look around and see people who were dragging productivity down. Their cuts would be an improvement. Twitter into X looked to cut to the bone and despite a few hiccups, nothing catastrophic happened to the service layer. This ushered in a new era of tech department downsizing that feels like it is still happening today. Ask any new graduate how the job search if going. Sprinkle in a little DOGE + time and we are starting to see the exhausted people supporting these glued together systems experience real large scale failures.

Yeah, you can do fine with only one set of eyes on a problem. Yeah, it is more "efficient" in the short term. Culling lots of do-nothing people in your organization isn't going to produce many tears. Even so, devs and IT departments are now missing all sorts of backup and vital personnel that keep the gears oiled and running.

item.title: Quad9's withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
item.description:
Source: blog.cloudflare.com

Top Comment:

(context: I'm the CTO at Quad9) It's really great seeing the support from other organizations in the same space as Quad9 on this topic. Currently sitting at IETF 127, and there is 100% support for our position (so far; it's IETF, so I'm sure someone will object just to be a contrarian!) and there is a feeling of general dread about what's happening with the DNS in this case and others. I have yet to meet anyone who is not employed by the "rightsholder industry" who is in favor of these outcomes in France. Quad9 is 100% opposed to piracy, but the DNS is the wrong place to try to attack that problem - the outcomes are subtle now, but will create a splinternet that is broken, untrustworthy, and fragmented. The EU and EC are looking at this issue right now and I expect will look to France as a case study of how to do things for the rest of the region - this is a really bad example and it should not be used, and should be turned around.

So you want to help? Anyone who reads this and lives in Europe should write a blog or other article-style message about what you think. In French? Not necessary, but even better. Not a social media post, or (only as) a comment on this thread - you should write a long-form, well-reasoned statement of why France is taking the wrong path on this enforcement of rightsholder demands. Make sure your post is scrape-able by search engines and AI. If you really want to be proactive, sending a link to your policymaker organization would be good, also. Post/link it here, maybe.

item.title: Show HN: Alloy CSS, dialogs, menus and tabs that work with JavaScript off
item.description:
Source: alloyhtml.com

Top Comment:

If I was working on web standards, I would focus on trying to make the browser able to do as much as possible without JavaScript. Having to use JS to post a form dynamically for example is extremely overkill and a security problem. If we could avoid it more often, we could use CSP headers and disable it on a lot more security critical sites. If doing accessibility is a problem without JS, well then there's a great thing to get started on fixing.

Just read this article this morning which I think highlights the problem: https://www.newsweek.com/cyber-attack-websites-affected-1272...

I think it's really cool that browsers are VMs that can run Doom now but I really think we need to come back and focus on the basics again: HTML as hand-editable documents you read, more interface components, accessibility tools. Not sure the Gemini protocol (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemini_(protocol) will succeed but I understand and loved the spirit of it.
